source.lineage: 1920s-onward Zulu South African male a-cappella vocal-group tradition (the name derives from the Zulu word cathama, to tread softly) that developed among Zulu migrant labourers in the Johannesburg mining hostels — codified through Solomon Linda Mbube 1939 recording (the recording that became The Lion Sleeps Tonight after a tortured rights-acquisition history), Ladysmith Black Mambazo (founded 1960 by Joseph Shabalala, the internationally famous group through their Paul Simon Graceland 1986 collaboration), and the broader Friday-night isicathamiya competition circuit in Johannesburg

extras.description: Isicathamiya (codified 1920s-onward in KwaZulu-Natal and Witwatersrand-Johannesburg South African mining-hostel weekend competition circuit, with Solomon Linda's 1939 Mbube Gallo Studios recording of the song that became The Lion Sleeps Tonight establishing the "mbube" subgenre name and the broader genre crystallizing through 1940s-1960s competition tradition; later international codification through Ladysmith Black Mambazo founded 1964 and Paul-Simon-collaboration 1986 Graceland-album breakthrough), the Zulu South African a-cappella male-vocal-group tradition. Cultural origin in Zulu rural-traditional choral practice (amahubo war-songs, izibongo praise-poetry, ingoma dance-songs) translated into urban-mining-hostel context where Zulu migrant laborers preserved cultural identity through weekend musical competition. Distinguished from preceding rural Zulu choral tradition by tighter ensemble-choreography and competition-format performance practice; distinguished from contemporary maskandi by a-cappella-not-guitar instrumentation; distinguished from later mbaqanga by absence of instrumental backing and pre-electric era foundation. source.name: Frevo
source.lineage: Brazilian Pernambuco (Recife) carnival fast-tempo brass-band marcha tradition codified 1907-onward as the working-class-and-capoeira-defense response to the elite-elite carnival-club tradition. extras.description: The Brazilian Rio Carnaval samba-school enredo (samba-enredo, "theme-samba") tradition continuous from 1928 first samba-school Deixa Falar foundation through the 1930s-1980s Estação Primeira de Mangueira and Portela canonical-school era into modern Sambódromo-procession continuous practice; the enredo is the canonical annual samba composition that narrates the parade-school's annual theme (each samba-school competing in the Sambódromo selects a yearly enredo theme — historical, cultural, mythological — and the entire parade is built around it). Defined by call-and-response puxador-and-bateria-and-crowd vocal arrangement, cavaquinho-and-tamborim-and-pandeiro-and-surdo bateria-ensemble (300-400 percussionists in major schools), Brazilian-Portuguese text register, samba 2-4 telecoteco rhythmic vocabulary, characteristic Sambódromo-procession context with parade-school competing for the championship.
